name: Carlos Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in-house at Harlow Pet Foods, mostly on the dog food range. My day starts with the numbers from yesterday's social posts and the online shop, then I'm writing: bag copy, emails to pet owners, scripts for the little videos our vets record. After lunch it's planning, like which flavour we push in spring and how much we spend on which channel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a line lands. We once changed 'grain-free' to 'nothing your dog doesn't need' on one bag and sales on that bag went up noticeably. What wears me out is approvals: legal, the vets, the regional sales lead, all with their red pen. I use the AI chat tool now and then for subject lines, but mostly I still write myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. Some people at work would be quietly glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and not much more, which is what I've been saying anyway. Online I wouldn't post about it, I mostly post football and my sister's dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means life carries on. I've got about ten months of costs saved in an index fund, I rent a flat I can afford, and there are pet brands and agencies all over this city. If Harlow went bad, I'd find something in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep using the chat tool for subject lines, because it does save me twenty minutes a day. I'd keep putting four hundred a month into the fund. And I'd start looking at buying a small flat in the next two years, since rent goes up every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. A bit bored by the whole debate, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your routine tasks would the tool take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The product listing text for the online shops and the reports from the social numbers. Those are hours of copy-paste. I'd happily give them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in your life you're worried about regardless of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mainly. My landlord put the rent up nine percent last spring. Buying a flat matters to me because of rent, not because of robots.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and not much more.
I'd keep posting **football** and my sister's dog, not AI takes.
think: Life carries on, with **ten months** of costs saved.
If Harlow went bad I'd find **another job** in a month.
do: Keep using the chat tool for **subject lines**, saving twenty minutes daily.
Keep putting **400 a month** into the index fund.
Start looking to **buy a flat** within two years.
feel: **Comfortable**, and a bit bored by the whole debate.
S0.quote: My landlord put the rent up nine percent last spring. Buying a flat matters to me because of rent, not because of robots.
fieldNote: His only pressure is **rising rent**, which he plans around.
Money and **local demand** keep him genuinely secure here.
He uses AI **lightly** and sees it as a small time-saver.

steps.text: Keep using the chat tool for Harlow email subject lines
Put 400 a month into the index fund
Start viewing small flats to buy within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that one feels close. We already had a talk about it at the team away day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who learn the tools will be fine and people who don't will struggle. That's the sensible middle, and I'd say it in the team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in the middle of the pack. I'm not the best writer at Harlow and I'm not the AI person either. In the middle of the pack is where the cuts land. If they need two of us instead of five, they keep Grace, who's brilliant, and Femi, who already builds the AI workflows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the paid online course our head of marketing keeps mentioning, the one on AI for content teams, and actually finish it. I'd volunteer to run the AI trial on the cat food range so my name is on it. And I'd hold off on buying the flat for a year until I know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. Like when the team gets a calendar invite with no title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis, honestly. He's 52, writes the vet scripts, and he's lovely. He's the slowest of us with new software. If anyone's going, I'm scared it's him first, then me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel you'd done enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If by the end of the year I'm the person running the cat food trial and it works, I'd breathe out. If Femi runs it and I'm just writing alongside, I'd start applying elsewhere.

say: I'd say people who **learn the tools** will be fine.
I'd put this **sensible middle** line in the team meeting.
think: I'm in the **middle of the pack**, where cuts land.
If they keep **two of five**, I'm probably not one.
do: Finish the paid **AI for content teams** course this year.
Volunteer to run the **cat food AI trial** myself.
Delay buying the **flat** by a year.
feel: **Uneasy** turning into worried, like an untitled meeting invite.
S1.quote: I'm not the best writer at Harlow and I'm not the AI person either. In the middle of the pack is where the cuts land.
fieldNote: He maps the team clearly and places himself **at risk**.
His fix is to put his **name on a trial**, a visible bet.
Worry for **older colleague Dennis** shows real care.

steps.text: Finish the paid AI for content teams course this year
Volunteer to run the AI trial on the cat food range
Put off buying a flat for one year
Apply to other brands if Femi gets the cat food trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments to slow it down and get some plan in place. At work I'd say we should be honest with each other about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is gone. Everything I do is on a screen: writing, planning, reading numbers. If a machine does all of that better by 2028, Harlow keeps maybe one person to sign things off, and it won't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop all big spending and drop the flat completely, and cut the gym and eating out. I'd keep the ten months in the fund and add to it. Then I'd look hard at work that needs people in a room: trade marketing, where you go round pet shops and vet clinics setting up displays. That's hands on, so it gets maybe three more years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Cold in my stomach. I'm 27 and I'd just got good at this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Abena (his sister) she's lucky to be a nurse, and I'd mean it. Then I'd probably ask if I can sleep on her sofa if it all goes wrong, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three more years in trade marketing. Is that a plan or a delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a delay, yeah. Trade marketing is a delay, not a plan. But three years with a wage and ten months saved is better than nothing. I'd use it to work out the next thing, whatever that is.

say: I'd say governments need to **slow it down** and plan.
At work I'd ask colleagues to be **honest** about what's coming.
think: My **job is gone**, because everything I do is on a screen.
Harlow might keep **one person** to sign off, not me.
do: Drop the **flat purchase** and stop big spending.
Keep and add to the **ten months** in the fund.
Move into **trade marketing**, setting up displays in pet shops.
feel: **Cold** in my stomach, because I'd just got good at this.
S2.quote: Trade marketing is a delay, not a plan. But three years with a wage and ten months saved is better than nothing.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** outright within two years.
The **hands-on gap** before robots is what he reaches for.
He's honest that the move is a **delay**, not a solution.

steps.text: Stop big spending and drop the flat purchase
Cut the gym and eating out to add to savings
Keep adding to the ten-month fund
Apply for trade marketing roles visiting pet shops and vet clinics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to prepare, not panic. I might even write something on my work profile about it, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it still ends my writing job, just later. But five years is enough to get properly good at one thing a machine can't do quickly, and to save a lot more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years becoming the AI person on the team, because that keeps me paid and teaches me how these things fail. Then I'd move toward trade marketing or partnerships with vet clinics, building actual relationships. I'd also buy a small flat after all, but a cheap one, so the mortgage is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It's a deadline, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy the flat now, if the job might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent keeps going up, and a small mortgage is cheaper than my rent. If I lose the job, I'd rather owe a little on something I own than keep paying a landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the vet clinics give you that the screen doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Trust, I think. Vets trust the rep who turns up every month and remembers their dog's name. That's slow to replace, even with clever software.

say: I'd say it's time to **prepare, not panic**.
I might even post about it on my **work profile**.
think: It still **ends my writing job**, just later.
Five years is enough to **save a lot** and get good at something.
do: Become the team's **AI person** for the first two years.
Move toward **vet clinic partnerships** after that.
Buy a **cheap flat** with a low mortgage.
feel: **Worried** but able to breathe, like a deadline, not a cliff.
S3.quote: Vets trust the rep who turns up every month and remembers their dog's name. That's slow to replace, even with clever software.
fieldNote: Time turns his fear into a **two-step plan**.
He still expects the **writing job to end**, so mood stays anxious.
Buying the flat is a **hedge against rent**, not a bet on the job.

steps.text: Run Harlow's AI writing tools for the next two years
Move into partnership work with vet clinics
Buy a cheap flat with a mortgage below his rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it. People would be talking about it at every leaving do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is plenty for me. I'd be 37, and by then I want to be managing people or relationships. The job I have now ends either way. With ten years, I can be gone from writing bag copy long before it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time master's in brand management over two years, paid partly by Harlow if they'd let me. I'd buy the flat, keep saving four hundred a month, and aim to move into a team lead role within five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small worry at the back, but it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does managing people get safer with AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not safe, no. But managing people means dealing with people, and I think that lasts longer. Honestly, I don't know. Nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the money got tight anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The football trips. I go to two away games a season and it's not cheap. That would go before the savings would.

say: I'd say we've got a **decade**, so let's use it.
It would come up at every **leaving do**.
think: Ten years is **plenty** for me, and I'd be 37.
I can leave **bag copy** long before it ends.
do: Do a **part-time master's** in brand management, partly paid by Harlow.
Buy the flat and keep saving **400 a month**.
Aim for a **team lead** role within five years.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a quiet worry at the back.
S4.quote: The job I have now ends either way. With ten years, I can be gone from writing bag copy long before it does.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him see a **career ladder**, not an exit.
He admits **nobody knows** whether managing people stays safe.
Football trips are the first **cut**, savings come last.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in brand management, partly paid by Harlow
Buy a small flat in the next year
Keep saving 400 a month into the index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't long enough to become anything else. What would help is honest notice from Harlow, and some kind of support to retrain, like a fund or a tax break for courses, so people like me move early instead of waiting for the letter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people around us. I'm fine on money. My workmate Dennis is 52 with a mortgage, and he isn't fine. I keep thinking about Dennis more than me.

headlineQuote: I'm fine on money. My workmate Dennis is 52 with a mortgage, and he isn't fine. I keep thinking about Dennis more than me.
portrait: Carlos, 27, writes **dog food copy** and plans campaigns in-house at Harlow Pet Foods.
He has **ten months saved** in an index fund and worries mostly about rising rent.
In Steady Disruption he sees himself in the **middle of the pack**, where cuts land.
In AGI by 2028 he expects to **lose his job** and would move into trade marketing.
With more time he plans a **master's** and a team lead role, and feels mostly okay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't long enough to become anything else.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest notice** from his employer and help paying for **retraining**.
